title: Swollen Feet After Drinking: Causes, Fixes, and When to Worry
excerpt: Why your feet and ankles swell after drinking, how to bring the swelling down fast, and the one-sided swelling and pain signs that mean you should see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why feet and ankles swell after drinking, how to reduce the puffiness fast, and the warning signs (one swollen leg, gout, chest pain) that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** puffy feet and ankles the morning after drinking are common and usually harmless. They come mostly from a fluid and salt shift: alcohol makes you lose water at first, your body then holds on to water and salt to make up for it, and gravity pools that extra fluid in your lower legs, especially if you stood, sat, or danced for hours and ate salty food. This kind of swelling affects both feet about equally, isn't very painful, and fades within a day or so.

**The quick rules:** Drink water, go easy on salt, put your feet up above the level of your heart, and move around. If both feet are mildly puffy and you feel otherwise fine, it should settle by the next day. If only **one** leg or foot is swollen, if a joint (often the big toe) is suddenly red, hot, and very painful, or if swelling keeps coming back every time you drink, don't wait it out. Those patterns point to something other than a simple fluid shift, and the section on when to see a doctor below explains why.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information for social drinkers, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to an emergency room** if leg swelling comes with chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing up blood, or fainting. **See a doctor the same day** if one leg is swollen, warm, red, or painful (especially the calf), if a joint is suddenly hot, red, and too painful to touch, if you have a fever with a red, spreading patch of skin, or if you can't put weight on your foot after a fall you may not remember clearly. **Book a regular appointment** if both feet swell often, if swelling lasts more than two or three days, if pressing on the skin leaves a dent that stays, or if you also notice a swollen belly, yellow skin or eyes, unusual tiredness, or getting short of breath lying flat. If you drink heavily most days and want to cut back, talk to a doctor first, because stopping suddenly after long-term heavy drinking can be unsafe without medical guidance.

## Why Do My Feet Swell After Drinking Alcohol?

Swelling in the feet and ankles is called **edema**. It means fluid has moved out of your blood vessels and settled in the tissue under your skin. Feet and ankles are the usual spot simply because they're the lowest part of your body for most of the day, so gravity pulls fluid there. After a night of drinking, several things push in the same direction at once.

### 1. The dehydration-then-rebound effect

Alcohol lowers the release of **vasopressin**, also called antidiuretic hormone. This is the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, your kidneys let more water go, which is why you visit the bathroom so often while drinking. Our guide on [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee) explains that part in detail.

The swelling usually shows up later. Once the alcohol wears off, your body notices it's short on water and swings the other way. It releases more water-saving hormones and holds on to fluid and sodium to restore balance. If you then drink a lot of water, eat salty food, and spend the day sitting, some of that retained fluid ends up in your lower legs. That is why you can feel dehydrated (dry mouth, headache) and look puffy at the same time. It sounds contradictory, but it's two phases of the same correction. For more on how much alcohol actually dries you out, see [does alcohol dehydrate you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### 2. Salt, and lots of it

Bar snacks, pizza, fries, wings, chips, and late-night takeout are among the saltiest foods most people eat. Sodium holds water in your body. When you eat a big load of salt, your body keeps extra water to dilute it, and that fluid has to go somewhere. Mixers and some cocktails (think Bloody Marys with a salted rim) add more. Salt is often the single biggest reason feet look swollen the next morning, more than the alcohol itself.

### 3. Alcohol widens your blood vessels

Alcohol relaxes and widens blood vessels, especially the small ones near the skin. That's why drinking can make your face flush and your skin feel warm. Wider vessels in your legs, combined with gravity, make it easier for fluid to seep out into the surrounding tissue. Heat makes this worse, so a hot bar, a summer barbecue, or a beach vacation adds to the effect.

### 4. Hours on your feet, or hours not moving

Your calf muscles act like a pump. Every time you walk, they squeeze the veins in your legs and push blood back up toward your heart. When you stand still at a party for hours, or sit for a long time at a dinner, on a plane, or in a car, that pump barely works. Blood and fluid pool in the lower legs. Then you often go straight to bed, sleep heavily, and don't move much. Dancing is different, because you're working your calves, but long periods on your feet in tight shoes still add up.

### 5. Inflammation

Heavy drinking triggers a general inflammatory response in the body, which is one of the ways researchers think hangovers make you feel ill. Inflammation makes small blood vessels a little leakier. On its own this is a minor contributor to foot swelling, but it adds to the other four factors.

## Swollen Ankles After Drinking

Swollen ankles after drinking come from exactly the same causes as swollen feet. The ankle is just where you notice it first, because the bony shape disappears and your socks leave deep marks. The same fixes apply: water, less salt, elevation, and movement.

One quick check: press your thumb firmly into the swollen area for about five seconds and let go. If it leaves a dent that slowly fills back in, that is called **pitting edema**. A small, short-lived dent the morning after a salty night out isn't unusual. Deep dents, or dents that you find often even when you haven't been drinking, are worth mentioning to a doctor, because regular pitting edema can be a sign of a heart, liver, kidney, or vein problem.

## Swollen Legs After Drinking

If the swelling runs up past your ankles into your shins or calves, the same fluid-shift explanation can still apply after a particularly big night, a long flight, or a hot day. But widespread leg swelling is less typical of a simple hangover. If both legs swell noticeably after drinking more than once, or if the swelling is slow to go away, it's a good reason to get checked. Long-term heavy drinking can affect the liver, the heart muscle, and the kidneys, and all three can show up first as swelling in the legs (more on that below).

## One Swollen Foot After Drinking: Don't Ignore It

Fluid-shift swelling is almost always **symmetrical**. Both feet look roughly the same. When only one foot, ankle, or leg is swollen, the cause is usually something local to that limb. These are the main possibilities:

### Gout

Gout is a type of arthritis caused by crystals of uric acid forming in a joint. A gout attack often starts suddenly, frequently at night, and typically hits the big toe, though it can also affect the ankle, the top of the foot, or the knee. The joint becomes hot, red, swollen, and extremely painful. Many people say even a bedsheet touching it hurts.

Alcohol is a well-known gout trigger. It raises uric acid levels in the blood and makes it harder for the kidneys to clear uric acid. Beer is a particular culprit because it also contains purines, which the body turns into uric acid. A big night of drinking plus a rich, meaty meal is a classic setup for a first attack. Gout needs a proper diagnosis and treatment, so see a doctor. Leaving it untreated can lead to repeated attacks and joint damage.

### An injury you didn't notice

Alcohol dulls pain and slows reaction time. It's easy to roll an ankle on a curb, stub a toe, or get stepped on and not register it until the next morning. A sprain or small fracture causes swelling on one side, often with bruising and pain when you put weight on it. If you can't walk on it, or the pain is getting worse, get it looked at.

### A skin infection (cellulitis)

Cellulitis is a bacterial skin infection that makes an area red, warm, swollen, and tender, and the redness can spread. It can start from a small cut, blister, or crack in the skin, including from new shoes on a night out. A fever or a red area that's growing needs a doctor promptly, because cellulitis usually needs antibiotics.

### A blood clot (DVT)

A deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is a blood clot in a deep vein, most often in the calf or thigh. Signs include swelling in one leg, pain or tenderness (often in the calf), warmth, and red or darker skin. Long periods without moving, such as a long flight or a long car ride, raise the risk. Dehydration is also commonly listed as a risk factor, so a long-haul flight with a few drinks and little water and little walking is a combination worth taking seriously.

DVT matters because a piece of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs (a pulmonary embolism), which is a medical emergency. **If one leg is swollen and painful, see a doctor the same day. If you also have chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, or cough up blood, call 911.**

## Swelling That Keeps Coming Back: When Drinking Habits Matter

Occasional puffiness after a big night is normal. Swelling that happens most times you drink, or that hangs around for days, is different. Several health conditions can cause leg and foot swelling, and some of them are linked to regular heavy drinking.

- **Liver disease.** The liver makes albumin, a protein that helps keep fluid inside your blood vessels. When the liver is badly damaged, as in cirrhosis, albumin levels can fall and pressure builds in the veins that drain the gut. Fluid then leaks into the legs and the belly. Swollen legs plus a swollen belly, yellow skin or eyes, or easy bruising are reasons to see a doctor soon. Our guide to [liver pain after drinking](/never-hungover/liver-pain-after-drinking) covers other liver warning signs.
- **The heart.** Long-term heavy drinking can weaken the heart muscle, a condition called alcoholic cardiomyopathy. A weaker heart pumps less well, and fluid backs up into the legs and lungs. Warning signs include swelling in both legs, getting out of breath easily, needing extra pillows to breathe at night, and a racing or irregular heartbeat. If your heart often pounds after drinking, see [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).
- **Blood pressure.** Regular heavy drinking is linked to higher blood pressure, which strains the heart and kidneys over time. Our [alcohol and blood pressure guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) explains the connection.
- **The kidneys.** Kidneys control how much salt and water your body keeps. When they aren't working well, fluid builds up, often first around the ankles and the eyes.
- **Vein problems.** Weak valves in the leg veins (chronic venous insufficiency) let blood pool in the lower legs. Alcohol's vessel-widening effect and long periods standing can make the swelling more obvious, even if alcohol isn't the root cause.

None of this means a puffy foot after a wedding is a sign of liver failure. It means that if the pattern is frequent or doesn't clear, a doctor can run simple tests (blood pressure, blood work, a urine test, and a heart and leg check) and either reassure you or catch something early.

## Medications That Can Make the Swelling Worse

Some common medicines cause ankle swelling on their own, and drinking can add to it.

- **Amlodipine and similar blood pressure pills.** Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine are well known for causing ankle swelling as a side effect. Alcohol also lowers blood pressure in the short term and widens blood vessels, so the two can stack up. Our [amlodipine and alcohol](/never-hungover/amlodipine-and-alcohol) page goes through the interaction.
- **NSAID painkillers.** Ibuprofen and naproxen can make the body hold on to salt and water. Taking them for a hangover headache after a salty night out can add to puffiness. They also irritate the stomach, which alcohol already does.
- **Steroids and some diabetes medicines.** Corticosteroids like prednisone and some diabetes drugs (such as pioglitazone) can cause fluid retention.
- **Hormonal medicines.** Estrogen-containing birth control and hormone therapy can cause mild fluid retention in some people.

Don't stop a prescribed medicine because of swelling. If you think a medicine is making your feet swell, especially when combined with drinking, talk to your doctor or pharmacist. There's often an alternative or a dose change that helps.

## How to Get Rid of Swollen Feet After Drinking

For ordinary, both-feet, morning-after puffiness, these steps help the fluid move back where it belongs. Most people see a clear improvement within a few hours and full recovery within a day or so.

### Elevate your feet

Lie down and rest your legs on a few pillows so your feet are higher than your heart. Gravity now works in your favor and helps fluid drain back up. Even 20 to 30 minutes, a few times during the day, makes a visible difference.

### Move your legs

A short walk is one of the best things you can do. It switches the calf-muscle pump back on. If you're stuck at a desk or on a plane, point and flex your feet, roll your ankles, and stand up every hour or so.

### Drink water, steadily

It feels backwards to drink more water when you're already holding fluid, but rehydrating tells your body it no longer needs to hoard water. Sip steadily through the day rather than chugging a liter at once. If you're also dealing with a headache or nausea, an electrolyte drink can help, though many sports drinks are salty, so a lower-sodium option or plain water with food may suit swelling better. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) compares the options.

### Cut back on salt for the day

Skip the salty hangover breakfast if you can, or at least balance it. Choose fresh foods over processed ones, and avoid adding salt. This lets your kidneys get rid of the extra sodium, and the water goes with it.

### Eat potassium-rich foods

Potassium helps the body balance sodium and supports normal fluid handling. Bananas, potatoes, avocados, oranges, leafy greens, beans, yogurt, and coconut water are good sources. Read [potassium and alcohol](/never-hungover/potassium-and-alcohol) for more on how drinking affects potassium levels. (If you have kidney disease or take medicines that raise potassium, check with your doctor before loading up on it.)

### Try compression socks

Light compression socks, the kind sold for flights and for people who stand all day, gently squeeze the lower legs and help stop fluid from pooling. They're especially useful for long flights, long work shifts, and weddings. Make sure they fit properly and aren't so tight they dig in. People with circulation problems in their legs or diabetes should ask a doctor before using them.

### Cool your feet

A cool (not icy) foot soak or a cool shower aimed at your legs can make swollen feet feel better and may ease the warmth and throbbing. Avoid hot baths and saunas while your feet are swollen, since heat widens blood vessels further.

### Take off tight shoes and socks

It sounds obvious, but tight shoes and socks with firm elastic bands can make swelling worse and leave painful marks. Loose, comfortable footwear helps while it settles.

## Is It Normal for Swelling to Last a Few Days?

Simple fluid-shift swelling usually peaks the morning after drinking and is gone within 24 to 48 hours, especially once you get moving and cut back on salt. If it's still there after two or three days, it's no longer a typical hangover symptom. Get it checked, especially if it's only on one side, if it's painful, or if you have other symptoms like breathlessness or a swollen belly.

## How to Prevent Swollen Feet Next Time

The best prevention is the same as for most hangover symptoms: drink less, drink more slowly, and look after your body while you do.

- **Alternate drinks with water.** A glass of water between alcoholic drinks slows your pace and blunts the dehydration-then-rebound swing.
- **Eat a real meal before you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Choose something that isn't extremely salty.
- **Go easy on salty bar snacks.** Fries, chips, pretzels, and wings add a lot of sodium in a short time.
- **Keep moving.** If you're standing at an event, shift your weight, walk around, and sit down for breaks. If you're sitting, stand up and stretch regularly.
- **Wear comfortable shoes.** Tight or high-heeled shoes for hours can make foot swelling and soreness worse.
- **Be careful on flights.** Long flights already cause foot swelling in many people. Adding alcohol, little water, and little walking makes it worse. Drink water, walk the aisle, and consider compression socks.
- **Put your feet up before bed.** A few minutes with your legs raised when you get home can reduce morning puffiness.

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them. If your face also looks puffy the next day, the same fluid shifts are at work, and [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) explains how to deal with it.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people add a supplement to their routine on nights out. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research is in animals and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven.

To be clear about this topic specifically: **there is no good evidence that DHM prevents or reduces foot swelling after drinking.** Foot swelling is mostly about salt, fluid balance, gravity, and movement, and the steps above address those directly. DHM also won't help gout, a blood clot, an injury, or any of the medical causes described earlier, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

If you're interested in trying DHM for general hangover support, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist first.

## The Bottom Line

Mildly swollen feet and ankles after drinking are usually a short-lived fluid and salt shift, made worse by gravity, heat, salty food, and long periods standing or sitting. Water, less salt, raising your feet, and a walk will usually clear it within a day. Swelling in only one leg, a hot and painful joint, swelling with chest pain or breathlessness, or swelling that keeps coming back are different. Those need a doctor, and the sooner the better.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do my feet swell after drinking alcohol?**

Mostly because of a fluid and salt shift. Alcohol makes you lose water at first, then your body holds on to water and sodium to recover, and gravity pulls that fluid into your feet and ankles. Salty food, heat, alcohol widening your blood vessels, and long periods standing or sitting all add to it. This kind of swelling affects both feet and usually clears within a day or so.

**How long do swollen feet last after drinking?**

Usually 24 to 48 hours. Most people notice a big improvement within a few hours of drinking water, cutting back on salt, raising their feet, and going for a walk. If swelling lasts more than two or three days, or keeps returning, see a doctor.

**Why is only one foot swollen after drinking?**

Swelling from a fluid shift almost always affects both feet. One swollen foot or leg points to a local cause, such as gout (often a hot, red, very painful big toe), an injury you didn't notice while drinking, a skin infection, or a blood clot. A swollen, painful calf on one side needs a doctor the same day, and chest pain or breathlessness with it means calling 911.

**Can alcohol cause gout in the feet?**

Alcohol is a common gout trigger. It raises uric acid levels and makes it harder for the kidneys to clear it, and beer adds purines that the body turns into more uric acid. A gout attack typically causes sudden, severe pain, redness, heat, and swelling in one joint, often the big toe. It needs a doctor's diagnosis and treatment.

**Does drinking water help swollen feet after alcohol?**

Yes. It sounds backwards, but rehydrating tells your body it no longer needs to hold on to extra water, and it helps your kidneys clear the extra salt. Sip steadily through the day, eat potassium-rich foods, and avoid very salty meals while the swelling settles.

**Are swollen ankles a sign of liver damage from drinking?**

Occasional puffy ankles after a big night are almost never a sign of liver damage. But swelling that happens often or doesn't go away, especially with a swollen belly, yellow skin or eyes, or easy bruising, can be a sign of liver disease in people who drink heavily. Heart and kidney problems can cause leg swelling too. If the pattern is regular, see a doctor for simple tests.

**Can my blood pressure medicine make swelling worse when I drink?**

It can. Calcium channel blockers like amlodipine commonly cause ankle swelling, and alcohol widens blood vessels and lowers blood pressure in the short term, which can add to it. NSAID painkillers like ibuprofen can also make you hold on to fluid. Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask your doctor or pharmacist about it.

**Does DHM help with swollen feet after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or reduces foot swelling. Swelling is mostly about salt, fluid balance, gravity, and movement, so water, less salt, elevation, and walking are what actually help. DHM is studied mainly for alcohol metabolism and liver health, and that research is still early.
